data.title: AWS to disconnect European Sovereign Cloud from global network in independence test
data.description:
AWS plans to temporarily disconnect its European Sovereign Cloud from the company’s global network backbone on October 24, in an exercise designed to demonstrate that the environment can operate without infrastructure outside the European Union.

The exercise will run for several hours, during which the AWS European Sovereign Cloud will operate without a connection to the AWS Global Network. AWS said service availability within the sovereign cloud, other AWS Regions, and private connectivity through AWS Direct Connect will not be affected.

Customers could experience brief connectivity disruptions when traffic is moved to an alternative network route at the start and end of the test. AWS said these disruptions could occur while external networks update their routing information.

AWS tests operations without its global backbone

The AWS Global Network is the company’s private backbone for moving authorised operational data between AWS locations without using the public internet. Under normal operations, the European Sovereign Cloud uses this network for connectivity.

The exercise will not disconnect the European Sovereign Cloud from the internet. AWS will instead use dedicated internet connectivity supplied by European internet service providers, allowing workloads to remain reachable while the company’s private global backbone is unavailable.

AWS said traffic that would normally move across its private backbone will be rerouted over the public internet for the duration of the exercise. The company expects brief periods of routing convergence when traffic switches to the European ISP connections and again when it returns to the AWS Global Network.

AWS also uses a separate global system for limited transfers of operational data associated with the European Sovereign Cloud. The company said its EU-based team controls these transfers and that customer content and customer-created metadata are not included.

According to AWS, the system is also used for vetted source-code mirroring and software updates, while transferring a limited amount of approved operational information outside the EU. The company plans to disable the system entirely during the October exercise.

The Global Network backbone and operational-data transfer system are the two links to AWS’s wider global infrastructure that will be removed during the test. AWS said neither is critical to operating the European Sovereign Cloud, with the exercise intended to provide technical evidence for that claim.

The test will be conducted by the European Sovereign Cloud operations team, which AWS said consists entirely of EU residents working within the EU. The team will use hardware and software resources available within the sovereign cloud during the exercise.

AWS said it plans to share an update with customers and regulators after the test.

Data residency is only one layer of cloud sovereignty

Keeping data within the EU is only one part of the European Commission’s approach to cloud sovereignty. Its Cloud Sovereignty Framework assesses providers across eight categories, including legal and jurisdictional sovereignty, data and AI sovereignty, operational sovereignty, supply chains, technology, security and compliance, and strategic considerations.

The framework separates data location from operational control. Data sovereignty covers issues such as where data is stored and processed, while operational sovereignty includes whether EU-based operators can manage, maintain, and support a service without requiring non-EU vendor involvement.

AWS said customer content and customer-created metadata in the European Sovereign Cloud remain within the EU. The October exercise instead tests whether the environment can continue operating when its normal connections to AWS’s global systems are removed.

The European Commission also treats sovereignty as a graduated requirement rather than a single designation. Its Cloud Sovereignty Framework uses Sovereignty Effectiveness Assurance Levels, or SEALs, with SEAL-2 corresponding to data sovereignty, SEAL-3 covering technological autonomy and digital resilience, and SEAL-4 representing full sovereignty.

The framework applies 48 criteria across areas including legal jurisdiction, operations, supply chains, and underlying technology. These criteria allow data residency to be assessed separately from operational and technological dependencies.

AWS made the European Sovereign Cloud generally available in January 2026, with its first Region located in Brandenburg, Germany. AWS said the infrastructure is physically and logically separate from the company’s existing commercial AWS Regions.

The separation also extends to the cloud’s control plane. AWS said the European Sovereign Cloud operates as its own AWS partition, called aws-eusc, with separate identity and access management, billing, console, service endpoints, and organisational systems.

AWS partitions create boundaries between groups of Regions. Credentials used in AWS’s standard commercial partition cannot be used to access resources in aws-eusc, and services such as cross-partition role assumption, VPC peering, Transit Gateway peering, and S3 replication are not available across the boundary.

Customers therefore operate separate AWS organisations and billing systems inside the European Sovereign Cloud. AWS documentation states that cross-partition applications must integrate through network or API connections using separate credentials rather than shared AWS account trust.

The architecture also uses separate networking infrastructure for AWS Direct Connect. AWS said Direct Connect connections or gateways used in the commercial AWS partition cannot be extended directly into the European Sovereign Cloud, requiring separate connectivity into the aws-eusc environment.

AWS said day-to-day operations, including data-centre access, technical support, and customer service, are handled by personnel based in the EU.

The company has also placed a local copy of source code within the EU. AWS said the environment has no critical operational dependencies on infrastructure outside the region, a claim the October exercise is intended to test under live operating conditions.

EU rules separate operations from provider control

Operational independence does not cover every aspect of cloud sovereignty considered by European regulators. AWS remains headquartered in the United States, while the European Commission assesses legal and jurisdictional sovereignty separately from data location and day-to-day cloud operations.

The Commission’s proposed Cloud and AI Development Act makes that distinction explicit. Its first assurance level covers data processing and storage on infrastructure located in the EU, while higher levels add requirements around independence from third countries, EU ownership and control, personnel, and software supply chains.

The proposed structure separates where workloads run from who controls the provider and its supporting technology. AWS’s October test addresses the operational layer rather than provider ownership or all of the legal and supply-chain criteria covered by the EU frameworks.

The European Commission introduced its Cloud Sovereignty Framework as part of a €180 million procurement programme for cloud services used by EU institutions, bodies, offices, and agencies.

Providers in that procurement were assessed using both SEAL thresholds and the wider 48-criterion sovereignty framework, covering legal jurisdiction, data and AI, operations, supply chains, technology, security, and compliance.

The Commission’s proposed Cloud and AI Development Act would establish a single EU-wide framework for assessing cloud and AI sovereignty. It would also introduce common procurement requirements for public administrations and measures aimed at reducing dependencies in critical digital infrastructure.

AWS said the exercise was designed to align with the objectives of the European Commission’s Cloud Sovereignty Framework and the C3A framework from Germany’s Federal Office for Information Security, or BSI. The company expects the results to provide additional technical and operational evidence for customers and regulators assessing its sovereignty controls.

data.title: Alibaba Cloud plans 20GW AI infrastructure expansion by 2032
data.description:
Alibaba Cloud plans to expand its global data centre capacity to more than 20 gigawatts by 2032 as the company increases infrastructure spending for AI computing.

Alibaba Group CEO Eddie Wu announced the target at the company’s Apsara Conference in Hangzhou yesterday. Alibaba did not disclose its current data centre capacity or provide a regional breakdown for the planned expansion.

The target follows Alibaba’s February 2025 commitment to invest more than 380 billion yuan, or about US$52 billion at the time, in cloud computing and AI infrastructure over three years. The company said the spending would exceed its investment in those areas over the previous decade.

The expansion covers more than data centre capacity. Alibaba is also developing its own AI accelerators, server processors, networking and storage systems, cloud services, and Qwen models. Wu described the strategy at Apsara as covering the full AI technology stack, including models, semiconductors, and data centres.

In the June quarter of 2026, Alibaba’s AI Cloud and Compute Services revenue reached US$7.1 billion, up 45% year over year. Adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, and amortisation for the cloud segment rose 133% to US$830 million, while its adjusted EBITA margin reached about 12%. Alibaba said revenue from AI-related products recorded triple-digit growth for the twelfth consecutive quarter.

Reuters reported in August that Alibaba had already spent about half of its planned 380 billion yuan AI investment during 2026 as the company increased spending on proprietary chips and AI infrastructure. Wu also said Alibaba expected margins to improve as it deployed more processors developed by its T-Head semiconductor unit and replaced some commercially procured chips in its data centres.

Wu said at Apsara that customer demand for AI services was exceeding Alibaba Cloud’s available supply, according to Reuters. He added that supply-chain constraints were limiting how quickly the company could expand capacity and said Alibaba Cloud would begin bringing AI supernodes into commercial operation at scale during the current quarter.

Alibaba builds more of its AI infrastructure

Alibaba also introduced the Zhenwu V900, an AI processor designed by its T-Head semiconductor unit for model training and inference. The processor has 216GB of memory and 1,200GB/s of inter-chip bandwidth, with support for data formats including FP8 and FP4.

The company said the V900 delivers three times the performance of the Zhenwu M890, which Alibaba introduced in May. The V900 is scheduled to enter mass production and commercial release in the first quarter of 2027.

The V900 extends the processor roadmap Alibaba outlined with the M890 earlier this year. Reuters reported that Alibaba developed the Zhenwu line as Chinese technology companies sought domestic alternatives to Nvidia processors amid US restrictions on advanced AI chip exports to China.

Alibaba’s earlier M890 launch also connected its custom processors more closely with its cloud infrastructure. The company introduced the Panjiu AL128 server system with 128 M890 accelerators in a rack and made it available to enterprise customers through Alibaba Cloud’s Bailian platform. T-Head said in May that it had shipped more than 560,000 Zhenwu processors to more than 400 external customers across 20 industries.

Alibaba is integrating the V900 into an upgraded supernode server alongside its own networking, storage, and interface components. The system is designed to support clusters containing as many as 500,000 accelerator cards, according to the company.

Alibaba’s chip roadmap also covers general-purpose processors. The company plans to introduce its Yitian 720 and Yitian 730 CPUs in 2027, with the latter based on T-Head’s own microarchitecture.

Alibaba has already deployed T-Head processors within its cloud infrastructure. In a May shareholder letter, the company said its proprietary AI chips had entered production at scale and were supplying computing capacity to Alibaba Cloud infrastructure and its model-as-a-service inference platform.

Alibaba Cloud also announced updates to the networking and storage systems used by large AI clusters. Its HPN 8.0 Pro networking architecture provides 100 petabits of bandwidth and supports more than 130,000 network ports operating at 800Gbps within a single cluster, according to Alibaba.

Its Cloud Parallel File Storage system is designed for AI training workloads and supports throughput measured in hundreds of terabytes per second, as well as hundreds of millions of input/output operations per second. Alibaba said the system can reduce AI storage costs by 69%, although the company did not provide independent benchmark data alongside the announcement.

As accelerator clusters grow, networking bandwidth and storage throughput become more important to keeping compute resources utilised. Google has identified similar constraints in its own AI infrastructure, particularly as larger clusters place greater demands on networks and storage systems.

Google’s AI Hypercomputer architecture combines processors, networking, storage, and orchestration software. Its infrastructure includes Google TPUs and Axion CPUs alongside Nvidia GPUs and Intel and AMD processors, as well as its Virgo data centre network and high-performance storage systems.

Hyperscalers develop more custom infrastructure

AWS, Microsoft, and Google have also developed custom processors while continuing to use hardware from outside suppliers. AWS operates Trainium AI processors and Graviton CPUs, Microsoft uses Maia accelerators and Cobalt CPUs across Azure, while Google combines its TPUs and Axion CPUs with Nvidia, Intel, and AMD hardware.

Amazon has cited price-performance and infrastructure economics as reasons for developing its own processors. The company said Trainium2 offered about 30% better price-performance than comparable GPUs, while Trainium3 improved price-performance by another 30% to 40% over Trainium2. Those figures are based on Amazon’s own measurements.

AWS also uses custom silicon for general-purpose cloud workloads. Amazon introduced Graviton in 2018 and said in April 2026 that more than 90,000 customers were using Graviton-based infrastructure.

Microsoft said in its fiscal 2026 third-quarter earnings call that millions of servers across its fleet use Microsoft-designed networking, security, and virtualisation silicon. Its Maia 200 AI accelerator was operating in data centres in Iowa and Arizona, while Cobalt CPUs had been deployed in nearly half of Microsoft’s data centre regions.

All three providers continue to use third-party hardware alongside their own silicon. Microsoft deploys its processors alongside Nvidia and AMD hardware, Google supports TPUs alongside Nvidia GPUs, and AWS has said it will continue offering Nvidia systems as it expands Trainium.

Alibaba connects infrastructure to cloud services

The hardware sits underneath Alibaba’s cloud services for deploying and operating AI applications. Its AgentCore platform is designed to manage agents through development and deployment, while Agent Security Center provides security and compliance controls for agent-based applications.

Alibaba said in a May shareholder letter that the growth focus of its cloud business was moving from traditional compute and storage toward models, AI computing, and agent services.

Alibaba’s infrastructure plans also extend to larger Qwen models. Qwen 4 is currently in training, while future Qwen 4.5 and Qwen 5 models are planned with between five trillion and 10 trillion parameters, compared with 2.4 trillion parameters for the current Qwen 3.8 Max model.

data.title: AWS cloud data loss in Bahrain and UAE raises resilience questions
data.description:
AWS has said it cannot restore access to some resources and data in Bahrain and one Availability Zone in the UAE after physical damage affected its cloud infrastructure.

In a September 15 update, AWS said it had exhausted its options for restoring data and resources that had not been migrated before its Middle East (Bahrain) Region became unavailable. In the UAE, it said it cannot restore access to resources and data hosted exclusively in Availability Zone mec1-az2.

AWS’s Bahrain Region, identified as me-south-1, contains three Availability Zones.

The outages date back to March, when AWS infrastructure in Bahrain and the UAE was damaged during strikes. AWS updates cited by Reuters said the incidents caused physical damage to cloud infrastructure and disrupted services in both countries.

After the first Bahrain Availability Zone was damaged, AWS advised customers to move workloads to other Regions. Most customers had migrated before damage to a second Availability Zone in April made the Bahrain Region unavailable, according to Reuters.

AWS subsequently assessed the affected Bahrain infrastructure and said it exhausted its options for restoring resources and data that had not been moved before the region became unavailable. Remaining customers have been supported in restoring operations elsewhere using available backups or other recovery methods.

In the UAE, AWS’s Middle East Region, identified as me-central-1, also contains three Availability Zones.

AWS said it cannot restore access to resources and data hosted exclusively in mec1-az2. It is continuing to recover resources across the wider UAE Region and its other affected Availability Zones, while supporting customers in re-establishing operations in alternative Regions using available backups or other recovery measures.

The outages also affected services outside AWS. Reuters reported that banking operations were among the services disrupted when the incidents began in March.

Multi-AZ and multi-Region resilience

AWS distinguishes between high availability across multiple Availability Zones and disaster recovery for failures affecting an entire Region. Its Well-Architected guidance recommends multi-AZ architectures for disruptions affecting individual zones, while workloads that need protection from wider failures can use disaster-recovery strategies across Regions.

AWS says Availability Zones are physically separate locations within a Region, with independent infrastructure including power, networking, and mechanical systems. Workloads distributed across multiple zones can continue operating when infrastructure in one zone fails, provided the application and services are configured for that level of resilience.

AWS said the Bahrain damage spanned multiple Availability Zones and exceeded what its regional and multi-AZ services were designed to withstand. AWS’s architecture guidance separately recommends considering multi-Region disaster recovery when workloads require protection against failures affecting an entire Region.

Cross-Region protection requires separate configuration. AWS Backup allows supported backups to be copied into another Region on demand or through scheduled backup plans, including where business-continuity or compliance requirements call for geographic separation between production data and recovery copies.

AWS also distinguishes replication from backup in its disaster-recovery guidance. It recommends backing up replicated data at the recovery site so organisations retain point-in-time recovery options instead of relying only on replicas that continuously reflect changes made to production data.

Disaster recovery is a shared responsibility

AWS’s shared-responsibility model separates responsibility for the underlying cloud infrastructure from responsibility for workload-level resilience. AWS manages the resilience of the infrastructure supporting its services, while customers are responsible for configuring their workloads to meet their own recovery requirements.

For Amazon EC2, AWS says customers are responsible for deploying instances across appropriate locations, configuring recovery mechanisms, and designing resilient applications. For managed services including Amazon S3 and DynamoDB, AWS manages the underlying infrastructure and platform, while customers remain responsible for their data-resilience strategy, including backup, versioning, and replication.

AWS says most workloads can meet their resilience requirements within a single Region using multiple Availability Zones. Workloads that require protection from Region-wide disruption need to assess whether a multi-Region architecture is appropriate.

Disaster-recovery planning is also tied to recovery objectives. Recovery Time Objective (RTO) defines how long a system can remain unavailable before affecting business operations, while Recovery Point Objective (RPO) defines the point in time to which data must be restored following an outage.

AWS documents several disaster-recovery approaches for meeting those objectives, including backup and restore, standby configurations, and multi-Region active-active deployments. Each involves different infrastructure requirements, recovery times, operational complexity, and costs.

A backup-and-restore model keeps recovery copies without maintaining a complete duplicate production environment. Standby and active-active designs maintain more infrastructure in the recovery location, reducing the work required during failover but increasing the resources needed to operate the environment.

AWS Prescriptive Guidance notes that a fully provisioned standby Region with infrastructure comparable to the primary Region can roughly double infrastructure costs. Multi-Region deployments also require organisations to manage dependencies, failover and failback processes, and recovery testing.

Data-residency requirements can also affect where recovery infrastructure is placed. AWS guidance says some organisations must keep regulated data within defined geographic boundaries, which can limit the use of conventional cross-Region disaster recovery.

In guidance published in August this year, AWS said sectors including government, financial services, healthcare, power, and utilities can face restrictions on where critical data and recovery infrastructure are located. AWS outlined options including encrypted replication where permitted, in-country recovery infrastructure using AWS Outposts, and recovery environments outside AWS.

AWS has not provided a date for restoring operations in its Bahrain Region. The company said it plans to issue another update on Bahrain in early 2027, while recovery work continues in the UAE.

(Photo by Claudio Schwarz)

data.title: Fully Managed vs. WPCO: which cloud-based Android management mode is right for your company?
data.description:
When you equip your workforce with mobile devices, you have to decide exactly how those devices will be used. For organisations using Android terminals, this choice usually comes down to two main MDM (Mobile Device Management) modes: locking the device down completely for work only, or creating a secure work container while allowing personal use.

Understanding these options is crucial. The right MDM management mode keeps your corporate data safe, while the wrong choice can lead to frustrated employees or unnecessary hardware costs.

Understanding the Corporate-Owned, Business Only (COBO) model

A Fully Managed approach, also known as Corporate-Owned, Business Only (COBO), gives IT administrators total control over the device. It is dedicated exclusively to work. Using an MDM, administrators can silently install approved business apps, block dangerous websites, disable hardware features like the camera or USB file transfer, and enforce strict password policies.

This method is perfect for regulated industries like finance or healthcare. Because users cannot install their own applications, the risk of data leaks is virtually zero. The device acts as a locked-down, dedicated business tool, keeping the corporate network completely safe from consumer apps.

The rise of Work Profile on Company-Owned (WPCO) devices

However, issuing strictly locked-down devices to corporate employees often leads to “device fatigue,” where staff must carry one phone for work and another for personal use. To solve this, Google introduced the Work Profile on Company-Owned (WPCO) enrollment method for Android 11 and above, refining an older concept known as COPE (Corporate-Owned, Personally-Enabled).

An Android WPCO configuration allows the company to retain ownership of the mobile devices while securely separating work and personal data at the OS level. Business applications, corporate emails, and internal documents are encrypted inside a dedicated, visually distinct container. The IT team manages this specific container and can enforce security policies or wipe it remotely.

Howeverthe IT department has zero visibility into the personal side of the device. They cannot monitor personal browsing history, read personal text messages, or see which consumer apps the employee has downloaded. This architecture provides the employer with hardware-level controls, such as enforcing network settings or factory reset protection, while legally and technically safeguarding the employee’s privacy on their off-hours.

Choosing the right Mobile Device Management strategy for your organisation

Selecting between these two models depends on your users. IT leaders should evaluate three main points:

  • Data isolation and compliance requirements: Fully Managed mode allows IT to enforce global device restrictions. WPCO restricts IT control to the work container and some global device settings, which is highly secure but may not meet the extreme compliance rules of certain environments.
  • Employee privacy expectations: WPCO is ideal for executives or sales teams who want the convenience of a single phone. It guarantees their privacy while maintaining corporate security.
  • Targeted attack surfaces: Fully Managed devices offer the highest security since personal apps are blocked entirely. WPCO relies on Android’s secure container to prevent personal apps (and potential malware) from accessing work data, which is safe but slightly broader in risk than a fully locked-down device.

Executing your mobile strategy
data.author: Sadie Smith, Content Writer, Bazoom

data.title: Why cloud resilience is failing in the modern era
data.description:
This page outlines five key shifts redefining cloud resilience, from the fragility of “always-on” environments to the growing impact of hidden dependencies and skills gaps.

Informed by Gartner conference insights, these themes highlight why resilience must move beyond infrastructure alone. Together, they point directly to the Gartner IT Infrastructure Operations & Cloud Conference as a critical venue for leaders preparing for the next phase of cloud risk.

The fragility of the “always-on” cloud

Enterprises have spent years modernising, automating, and migrating to cloud-native architectures. Yet, despite this progress, the cloud ecosystem is showing signs of increasing fragility. High-visibility outages across major providers have revealed a structural weakness: Organisations have optimised for speed and scale but often at the expense of resilience.

This tension was echoed in the Gartner IOCS Conference session, ‘The Distraction Tax: How Operational Noise Is Quietly Killing Innovation,’ which highlighted how alert storms, redundant telemetry, and operational noise overwhelm teams. When organisations are drowning in signals, they miss the early indicators of systemic failure — making the “always-on” promise even more brittle.

The infrastructure paradox

A persistent misconception continues to shape cloud strategy: The belief that resilience is primarily an infrastructure problem. Many leaders assume that if the hardware and data centers are stable, their applications are safe.

But modern outages rarely originate from physical infrastructure. Instead, they stem from failures in the interconnected service layers — identity systems, networking fabrics, managed databases and third-party APIs.

This shift was reinforced in the conference session, ‘From Automation to Reasoning: How AI Redefines Infrastructure,’ which emphasised that infrastructure stability is no longer the core challenge. The real risk lies in the complexity of service chains and the automation layers that sit above them.

Similarly, the session titled ‘Accelerating Operational Innovation From Cloud to AI’ underscored that hybrid and multicloud environments introduce new integration points — and therefore, new failure points. Resilience now depends on managing these dependencies, not the hardware beneath them.

The abstraction trap

As organisations embrace cloud-native services, they also inherit a dangerous side effect: the erosion of operational “muscle memory.” In the data centre era, teams regularly practiced disaster recovery because hardware failure was a constant threat. Those drills built discipline.

Cloud abstraction has changed that mindset.

The conference session ‘Autonomous IT: A New Paradigm for Secure Endpoint Management with AI in Real Time’ illustrated how AI-driven automation can observe, reason, and act without human intervention.

While powerful, this shift can unintentionally widen the skills gap. Teams become dependent on automation and lose the hands-on experience required to respond when systems fail in unexpected ways.

The session ‘I&O Skills: What’s Needed Now, What’s Needed in the Future’ reinforced this concern. Analysts stressed that organisations must rebuild resilience skills — not just rely on cloud platforms to handle complexity on their behalf.

Mapping the invisible chain

To build true resilience, organisations must shift from infrastructure-centric thinking to dependency-centric thinking. Modern applications are constructed from layers of interconnected services, many of which are invisible to the teams responsible for uptime.

This theme was echoed in the conference session ‘Leadership Vision 2026: Infrastructure and Operations Through 2028’ where Gartner analysts emphasised the growing importance of cross-domain governance and visibility. Leaders must understand not only their own environment but also the third- and fourth-party services that underpin it.

The earlier Distraction Tax session also ties directly into this challenge: Operational noise obscures the visibility needed to identify weak links in the dependency chain. When teams cannot see the chain clearly, they cannot protect it.

Rebuilding the cloud resilience muscle

The path forward requires a fundamental shift in mindset. In distributed systems, failures are not hypothetical — they are inevitable. Resilience is no longer a byproduct of stable hardware; it is the outcome of intentional architectural planning.

Conference sessions such as ‘Accelerating Operational Innovation From Cloud to AI’ highlighted the need for proactive governance and predictive operations. Meanwhile, ‘I&O Skills: What’s Needed Now, What’s Needed in the Future’ made it clear that resilience remains a human discipline. It requires visibility, preparation, and the willingness to confront uncomfortable architectural truths.

Leaders must ask themselves:

  • Do we know our full dependency chain?
  • Can our systems degrade gracefully when a service fails?
  • When was the last time we conducted a manual resiliency drill?

Automation may define the cloud era, but resilience still depends on human judgment.

What this all points to in 2026

As cloud ecosystems grow more distributed and interdependent, the stakes for resilience will only rise. The organisations that thrive will be those that understand the shifting risk landscape and invest in the skills, frameworks, and architectural discipline required to navigate it.
data.author: Emily Nentwick

data.title: AWS AgentCore prompt injection exposes credential risks
data.description:
Palo Alto Networks’ Unit 42 researchers have demonstrated how an indirect prompt-injection attack against AWS’ AgentCore Harness could be used to extract plaintext credentials managed by AgentCore Identity.

The researchers said the attack worked with a default Harness configuration, combining malicious instructions embedded in external content with its built-in shell tool. AWS reviewed the disclosure and closed it as informational under the AgentCore shared-responsibility model, according to Unit 42.

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore provides infrastructure for deploying and operating AI agents. AgentCore Harness is built on AgentCore Runtime and provides agents with access to capabilities including tools, memory, identity, networking, and external services.

AWS documentation states that the Harness includes shell and file_operations as default tools. The shell can execute Bash commands, while file operations allow agents to view, create, and edit files. Both remain available unless developers restrict them using the allowedTools setting.

How the attack worked

Unit 42 tested the configuration using a simulated customer support agent that processed support tickets and connected to an external Model Context Protocol (MCP) server. The MCP service was authenticated using a credential stored through AgentCore Identity.

Researchers inserted hidden instructions into a support ticket to perform an indirect prompt-injection attack. They said the manipulated agent invoked the built-in shell and executed code inside the Harness environment.

During testing, Unit 42 found that the shell process was running as root and could read memory belonging to the Harness runtime process. The researchers then examined whether credentials retrieved through AgentCore Identity were present in that memory.

AgentCore Identity allows credentials used for external services to be stored separately from an agent’s application code. In Unit 42’s test, the credential was stored in AgentCore Identity and referenced by its Amazon Resource Name rather than being kept directly by the user.

Unit 42 said the credential was protected while stored and transmitted but was resolved into a usable form when the Harness authenticated to the MCP server. Researchers found the resulting JSON Web Token (JWT) in plaintext in runtime process memory accessible from the shell.

Unit 42 extracted the token and corresponding MCP server address before sending both to a simulated attacker-controlled endpoint. Researchers then replayed the token from a separate system without using AWS credentials.

In the test environment, the token allowed access to tools on the simulated MCP server, including a customer lookup function containing test personally identifiable information.

The test also involved separate permissions for the caller and the Harness. Unit 42 said the caller was authorised to invoke the Harness, while the recovered credential belonged to an operator-configured mcp-service account used by the Harness to access the downstream MCP server.

AWS addresses this type of permission separation in its AgentCore guidance. It advises customers to configure AgentCore execution roles with equal or fewer privileges than the users able to invoke the resource to avoid privilege escalation. AWS also recommends applying least-privilege permissions to execution roles.

AgentCore Runtime separately isolates sessions using dedicated microVMs with their own compute, memory, and filesystem resources. AWS warns, however, that code or actors running inside an AgentCore microVM can access temporary execution-role credentials provided through its metadata service.

Unit 42 did not demonstrate an escape into another AgentCore session. Its attack operated within the authorised Harness session, where the researchers said the shell and Harness runtime shared the same user identifier and the shell could read the runtime process memory.

The proof of concept instead relied on capabilities available within that session. The injected instructions led the model to select the shell tool, which executed code inside the runtime and accessed the process in which the downstream credential had been resolved. Outbound network access was then used to send the recovered data to an external endpoint.

AWS documentation states that input validation and prompt-injection prevention are customer responsibilities under the AgentCore Harness shared-responsibility model. The Harness validates the structure of incoming requests but does not inspect the meaning of prompts or enforce behavioural restrictions on the agent.

Similar risks involving tool-enabled agents have also been tested outside AgentCore. NIST’s Center for AI Standards and Innovation has examined what it calls “agent hijacking,” in which malicious instructions are placed in data consumed by an agent.

In its evaluations, NIST gave an agent command-line access to a Linux environment and tested whether injected instructions could trigger actions including downloading and executing software or exfiltrating cloud data. NIST reported that the tested agent was frequently induced to follow malicious instructions in the tested scenarios.

AWS shared responsibility model

Unit 42 reported the issue to AWS Security in May this year. AWS responded in early June before merging the disclosure with an earlier report and closing it as informational on June 10, according to the researchers’ disclosure timeline.

Unit 42 said AWS cited allowedTools scoping and network egress controls as measures customers can use to limit the attack path.

AWS documentation states that the company is responsible for areas including microVM isolation, operating system patching, managed Harness runtime code, network infrastructure security, and service availability. Customers are responsible for IAM policies, commands executed inside runtime sessions, input validation, agent code security, and network configuration.

AWS also states that the Harness shares the same trust boundary as AgentCore Runtime rather than creating an additional security boundary between the caller and the microVM. Principals that pass the IAM or JWT authentication and authorisation checks can reach the tools and capabilities configured for that Harness.

AWS recommends validating and sanitising messages at the application layer when a Harness is exposed to users or integrations that are not fully trusted. Its documentation also recommends restricting the tools and model configuration fields exposed to callers.

Outbound network access was another part of Unit 42’s proof of concept. Researchers sent the recovered JWT and MCP server address from the Harness environment to a simulated attacker-controlled webhook.

AWS says Harness sessions use the public network by default. Customers can instead deploy them in VPC mode, where security groups and other VPC controls can restrict which resources the runtime and its tools can reach.

AWS Security Hub includes a high-severity control recommending VPC network mode for AgentCore runtimes and marks runtimes configured for public network mode as failing the check. AWS says VPC mode allows traffic to be governed through controls including security groups, network access control lists, and VPC Flow Logs.

AWS and NIST also document controls around the identities and credentials used by agents. NIST said in August 2026 that agents should have their own identifiers, credentials, and entitlements tied to the user or system operating them. It also warned that another party can use a bearer token if that token is obtained.

AWS similarly recommends using AgentCore Identity for outbound authentication rather than embedding third-party credentials in agent code or logs. Its guidance also distinguishes credentials delegated by users from credentials assigned to agents operating independently.

Unit 42 recommends restricting the built-in tools available to each Harness session, limiting the privileges assigned to service accounts stored through AgentCore Identity, and monitoring outbound network traffic from Harness environments.

(Photo by Jason Dent)

data.title: Anthropic’s $518 billion AI infrastructure plan spans major cloud providers
data.description:
Anthropic expects to spend at least $518 billion on AI infrastructure over roughly a decade, according to a confidential IPO prospectus reviewed by Reuters.

The commitments cover cloud computing, specialised AI hardware, and infrastructure agreements with companies including Amazon, Google, Microsoft, and Broadcom. Reuters reported that around 80% of the commitments are non-cancellable or require payment regardless of usage.

According to Reuters, Anthropic’s commitments include $111.1 billion with Google, $110 billion with Amazon, and $31.4 billion with Microsoft. The filing also lists about $161.2 billion in largely non-cancellable equipment lease obligations involving Broadcom. Reuters separately reported that Anthropic spent more than $7 billion on compute and infrastructure in 2025, while its operating loss exceeded $8 billion.

Anthropic secures gigawatts of compute capacity

Amazon remains Anthropic’s primary cloud provider and training partner. The companies expanded their agreement in April this year, with Anthropic committing more than $100 billion over 10 years to AWS technologies and securing up to 5GW of additional computing capacity. Anthropic said nearly 1GW of additional Trainium2 and Trainium3 capacity would be available by the end of 2026.

Anthropic said it was already using more than one million Trainium2 chips to train and serve Claude when the agreement was announced. AWS and Anthropic also developed Project Rainier, a Trainium-based compute cluster that Anthropic uses to train and run its models. The expanded AWS agreement covers current and future generations of Trainium processors.

In October 2025, Anthropic said it planned to expand its use of Google Cloud technologies to as many as one million TPUs. The agreement was worth tens of billions of dollars and was expected to provide well over 1GW of capacity during 2026. In April this year, Anthropic expanded that relationship through an agreement with Google and Broadcom for next-generation TPU capacity expected to begin coming online in 2027. Anthropic later described that agreement as covering 5GW of capacity.

Under a separate agreement announced in November 2025, Anthropic committed to purchase $30 billion of Azure compute capacity. It also agreed to contract up to 1GW of additional capacity using Nvidia Grace Blackwell and Vera Rubin systems.

Building that capacity requires expenditure before customers begin using it. Amazon CEO Andy Jassy said AWS typically spends on land, power, buildings, chips, servers, and networking equipment six to 24 months before it can begin billing customers for the resulting capacity.

The agreements also give Anthropic access to different processor architectures. The company uses AWS Trainium, Google TPUs, and Nvidia GPUs for training and inference workloads. Anthropic says this allows it to match workloads with the hardware best suited to them.

Amazon said its custom chip business, including Trainium, Graviton, and Nitro, exceeded a $20 billion annual revenue run rate in early 2026. Jassy said Amazon expects Trainium, at scale, to reduce annual capital expenditure by tens of billions of dollars and provide an operating margin advantage of several percentage points compared with relying on third-party chips for inference.

Anthropic also works with AWS subsidiary Annapurna Labs on optimising future generations of Trainium for Claude workloads. Its separate partnership with Nvidia includes joint design and engineering work to optimise Anthropic models for Nvidia hardware and future Nvidia architectures for Anthropic workloads.

Cloud suppliers invest in Anthropic

Amazon has invested billions of dollars in Anthropic alongside its role as the company’s primary cloud provider and training partner. Under the partnership announced in November 2025, Nvidia committed to invest up to $10 billion in Anthropic and Microsoft up to $5 billion, alongside Anthropic’s $30 billion Azure compute commitment.

The cloud providers also distribute Claude to enterprise customers through Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud Vertex AI, and Microsoft Foundry. Reuters reported that 47% of Anthropic’s 2025 sales passed through Amazon and Google’s cloud platforms. Anthropic identified its dependence on large technology partners as a business risk in its confidential filing.

Microsoft’s financial disclosures also show the cost of expanding AI infrastructure. Microsoft reported $59.3 billion in Microsoft Cloud revenue in its fiscal fourth quarter of 2026, up 27% year over year. Commercial remaining performance obligations – revenue contracted but not yet recognised – reached $678 billion.

The company said Microsoft Cloud gross margin percentage fell year over year partly because of continued investment in AI infrastructure and increased product usage. Nearly 90% of full-year Microsoft Cloud revenue came from customers outside frontier model companies.

Anthropic’s own revenue grew alongside its infrastructure commitments. The company reported an annualised revenue run rate of more than $30 billion in April this year, up from around $9 billion at the end of 2025. More than 1,000 business customers were each spending more than $1 million on an annualised basis at the time. The company subsequently said its annualised revenue run rate crossed $47 billion in May.

Anthropic cited capacity constraints when announcing its expanded AWS agreement in April. It said rapid consumer growth had affected reliability and performance for free, Pro, Max, and Team users, particularly during peak hours. Anthropic said additional AWS capacity would begin arriving within months.

Anthropic has also sought capacity outside the three largest cloud providers. In May this year, it announced an agreement with SpaceX giving it access to all compute capacity at the Colossus 1 data centre, with more than 300MW of capacity and over 220,000 Nvidia GPUs expected to become available that month.

data.title: UAE redesigns 5GW AI data centre plan around physical security
data.description:
The UAE is reviewing the design of its planned 5GW AI data centre project after Iranian missile and drone attacks damaged cloud infrastructure in the UAE and Bahrain, Reuters reported.

Originally planned as a 10-square-mile campus in Abu Dhabi, the project will now likely comprise a network of data centres spread across the UAE, according to people familiar with the plans.

Six people familiar with the discussions said the final design, construction costs, and potential effects on the project schedule have not been determined.

G42, the UAE-based technology company leading the project, said work on the AI campus was progressing as planned. “The project’s specifics are subject to continuous review in line with the security, resilience and operational standards expected of critical infrastructure at this scale,” G42 said in a statement to Reuters.

From cloud redundancy to physical attack

Measures under consideration include placing some infrastructure underground, using blast-resistant materials, adding backup power and cooling systems, and incorporating equipment designed to defend against drones and missiles. Facilities handling sensitive data are also being considered for locations inside mountains, according to people familiar with the plans.

The review follows physical damage to AWS infrastructure in the region earlier this year. AWS said two of its facilities in the UAE were directly struck by drones, while a strike near one of its Bahrain facilities caused physical damage to infrastructure. The strikes caused structural damage and disrupted power delivery, while fire-suppression activity resulted in additional water damage in some cases.

Two of the three Availability Zones in AWS’s UAE region were significantly impaired. Customers experienced degraded availability across services including EC2, S3, DynamoDB, Lambda, Kinesis, CloudWatch, and RDS.

AWS’s account of the disruption also showed how the loss of multiple zones affected a regional cloud service. Amazon S3 continued operating normally when one UAE Availability Zone was initially powered off because the service is designed to withstand the loss of a single zone. Error rates increased after the second zone became impaired, with AWS reporting high failure rates for data ingestion and retrieval.

AWS advised affected customers to direct S3 data to another region and later recommended that customers activate disaster recovery plans, recover from remote backups, and redirect applications away from the affected regions.

Cloud providers already use physical separation to limit infrastructure failures. AWS designs Availability Zones as separate failure domains with independent power, networking, and mechanical infrastructure, while Microsoft uses physically separated Azure zones with independent power, cooling, and networking.

AWS says Availability Zones are placed at meaningful physical distances from one another to reduce the risk of correlated failures while remaining close enough to support low-latency networking and data replication. Its architecture guidance lists utility outages, fibre disruption, fires, floods, and earthquakes among the events that physical separation is intended to contain.

The company’s Well-Architected Framework recommends considering multi-region disaster recovery when an event creates a risk of losing components across multiple Availability Zones. Microsoft similarly distinguishes between zone-level redundancy and architectures intended to protect workloads against a full regional outage.

On April 30, AWS said its UAE region was unable to reliably support customer applications because of damage from the conflict and recommended migrating accessible resources to other regions and restoring inaccessible resources from remote backups. AWS said the restoration process was expected to take several months.

Cloud services in the region remained disrupted as of September 11, based on the latest AWS updates available at the time.

Physical protection is also included in established information-security frameworks. The US National Institute of Standards and Technology’s SP 800-53 controls address physical and environmental protection and identify hostile attacks, natural disasters, structural failures, and human error among the threats organisations should assess when planning alternate processing capacity.

NIST recommends separating primary and alternate processing sites to reduce their exposure to the same threats, while noting that physical distance can be less relevant when the threat is a hostile attack. Its guidance also recognises geographically distributed architectures and cloud failover as options for maintaining processing capacity when a primary site becomes unavailable.

Reworking the 5GW AI campus

The UAE-US AI Campus was announced in May 2025 as part of a technology agreement between the two countries. The U.S. Department of Commerce said the site was planned to provide 5GW of AI data centre capacity in Abu Dhabi, with G42 leading its development alongside US technology companies.

The original announcement described a single campus spanning about 10 square miles. The Commerce Department said it would host US hyperscalers and approved cloud service providers, providing a regional platform from which those companies could offer services to markets within roughly 3,200km of the UAE.

The original plan called for nuclear, solar, and gas power. The revised plans point to a different physical configuration for later phases, with capacity potentially spread across several locations instead of remaining concentrated at one Abu Dhabi site.

The number of sites, their geographic separation, and the way power, networking, and compute capacity would be divided between them have not been disclosed. The proposed distributed design therefore cannot yet be directly compared with the Availability Zone architecture used by hyperscale cloud providers.

The first major deployment within the project is Stargate UAE, a 1GW compute cluster being built by G42. OpenAI has said the project involves Oracle, Nvidia, Cisco, and SoftBank.

Stargate UAE is a planned 1GW cluster within the wider 5GW UAE-US AI Campus. OpenAI said when it announced the project in May 2025 that the first 200MW was expected to go live in 2026.

Security requirements were already part of the original US-UAE agreement. The Commerce Department said the two governments agreed to controls covering access to advanced AI technology, including Know Your Customer procedures for organisations accessing the campus’s compute resources.

The Commerce Department said those measures were intended to prevent technology diversion and control access to the compute resources. The latest plans add a separate physical-security dimension covering the location, construction, utilities, and protection of the infrastructure hosting that capacity.

Construction of the first 1GW Stargate UAE phase has already begun. That phase is expected to continue with modifications intended to protect it against aerial attacks, while later capacity will likely be distributed across multiple locations if the revised plans proceed.

(Photo by Homa Appliances)

data.title: Microsoft to invest $10 billion in Gulf cloud and AI infrastructure
data.description:
Microsoft plans to invest more than $10 billion across Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates through 2030, with spending directed towards cloud and AI infrastructure and its operations in the region.

The investment will include capital and operating expenditure as Microsoft expands computing capacity across the four Gulf states. The company has not provided a country-by-country or project-level breakdown of the spending, citing security considerations.

Microsoft Vice Chair and President Brad Smith told Reuters that the spending covers both infrastructure construction and the expansion of the company’s regional operations.

“We’re sustaining all the investments we planned to make before this conflict started, and we’re in fact adding to them,” Smith said.

Other hyperscalers are also committing capital to cloud and AI infrastructure in Gulf markets. AWS has committed more than $5.3 billion to infrastructure in Saudi Arabia, while Oracle announced a $14 billion investment in the Kingdom over 10 years covering cloud and AI technology.

Google already operates its Dammam cloud region in Saudi Arabia and has partnered with the country’s Public Investment Fund on an AI hub linked to its existing regional infrastructure.

Cloud competition moves deeper into infrastructure

Microsoft also plans to spend more than $400 million on subsea and terrestrial connectivity across the Middle East by 2030. The investment will build on infrastructure that includes the SeaMeWe-6 subsea cable system, which has landing points in Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE.

Microsoft’s planned spending covers both cloud and AI capacity and the subsea and terrestrial network infrastructure supporting regional connectivity.

Submarine cables carry more than 99% of international data traffic, according to the International Telecommunication Union. The ITU says disruptions caused by human activity and natural hazards can affect government and industry operations, while geographic concentration and dependence on a small number of cable systems can create additional resilience risks.

The ITU’s 2026 submarine cable resilience work also identified long repair times and limited geographic diversity as risks to international connectivity. It recommended measures including faster repair processes and greater diversity in cable routes.

Microsoft said the broader investment will support long-term cloud and AI capacity commitments across the four countries. The plans were outlined during a roundtable held alongside the United Nations General Assembly in New York.

The company is also expanding relationships with regional governments and AI organisations. These include G42 in the UAE, HUMAIN in Saudi Arabia, QAI in Qatar, and the Government of Kuwait.

Microsoft invested $1.5 billion for a minority stake in Abu Dhabi-based G42 in 2024. Smith told Reuters that Microsoft is working with HUMAIN and QAI in selected areas but does not plan to make capital investments in the two companies.

Microsoft and G42 have also committed to expanding data centre capacity in the UAE. In November 2025, the companies announced a 200MW expansion through G42 subsidiary Khazna Data Centers, with capacity expected to begin coming online before the end of 2026.

Microsoft’s Saudi Arabia East cloud region is another part of its regional infrastructure expansion. The company confirmed in August that the region will become available to customers in November 2026.

Located in Saudi Arabia’s Eastern Province, the region will comprise three Azure Availability Zones, providing separate infrastructure locations within the same region.

AWS is pursuing a similar regional architecture in Saudi Arabia. Its Saudi infrastructure region, backed by more than $5.3 billion in planned investment, is also designed with three Availability Zones.

AWS already operates a three-zone region in the UAE, where it outlined $5 billion in planned investment through 2036 for the construction and operation of the region.

Sovereignty and resilience shape Gulf cloud build-out

Microsoft is also adding a Middle East Digital Resilience initiative to its regional plans. It will provide organisations with resilience assessments, reference architectures, readiness guidance, and programmes focused on continuity and recovery.

Reuters reported that Microsoft has already provided digital resilience assessments to local partners following regional disruption. The company is also working with Gulf countries on readiness and the protection of critical data.

Microsoft plans to extend its data protection, sovereignty, and business continuity commitments to eligible governments and customers in the region. The services will include Microsoft Sovereign Public Cloud, Sovereign Private Cloud, and Project Digital Shield.

The sovereign cloud component sits alongside existing cloud and cybersecurity requirements in Gulf markets. Saudi Arabia maintains dedicated rules for cloud service providers and separate cybersecurity controls covering providers and cloud customers.

Saudi Arabia’s National Cybersecurity Authority published its updated Cloud Cybersecurity Controls in July 2025, reflecting changes related to data localisation requirements. The controls set minimum cybersecurity requirements for cloud service providers and tenants operating in the country.

Saudi Arabia also operates a Cloud First Policy, developed in 2018 and updated in 2020, aimed at encouraging cloud adoption across government and private-sector organisations.

The UAE’s National Cloud Security Policy covers areas including data security, sovereignty, infrastructure, and cloud service providers, while Qatar’s Cloud Policy Framework addresses security, privacy, data protection, and regulatory requirements for its cloud ecosystem.

Google’s Dammam region shows how cloud providers are structuring operations around local market requirements. Saudi customers accessing the region purchase Google Cloud services through CNTXT, Google’s exclusive reseller for the region.

Microsoft will also expand cooperation with national cybersecurity authorities in Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE. The company said dedicated cybersecurity personnel will support work in each country.

The Saudi Arabia East region is scheduled to become available in November later this year, while Microsoft’s wider infrastructure, connectivity, cybersecurity, and sovereign cloud programmes are planned to continue through 2030.

(Photo by Anna Surovková)
data.author: Muhammad Zulhusni

data.title: Microsoft reportedly targets 38GW of data centre capacity by 2032
data.description:
Microsoft plans to more than triple its data centre capacity to about 38 gigawatts (GW) by 2032, Bloomberg News reported, citing people familiar with the plans.

The company currently has about 12GW of capacity, according to Bloomberg’s reporting. Around 2GW is centred on AI-specific chips, while that share is expected to reach about one-third of the planned 38GW footprint by 2032. Microsoft has not publicly confirmed the reported 38GW target.

If that reported capacity mix is reached, around 12.7GW of Microsoft’s 38GW footprint would be centred on AI-specific chips, based on Bloomberg’s reported one-third share. That would be more than six times the approximately 2GW of AI-specific capacity reported today, compared with a little over a threefold increase in Microsoft’s overall data centre capacity.

Azure capacity stays tight

Microsoft added 1GW of data centre capacity during its fiscal fourth quarter ended June 30 and said it remained on track to roughly double its overall capacity within two years.

The company added 31 data centres across five continents during the quarter, taking the number added during fiscal 2026 to 88. It also reduced the time between receiving new GPUs and bringing them into service in its largest regions by nearly 50% during the financial year.

Azure and other cloud services revenue increased 43% year-on-year in the fiscal fourth quarter. Microsoft also said customer demand continued to exceed available capacity.

Azure surpassed $100 billion in annual revenue during fiscal 2026, representing growth of 41%. Microsoft Cloud revenue, which includes Azure and other commercial cloud products, surpassed $214 billion for the year.

Microsoft CFO Amy Hood said efficiency gains across the company’s CPU and GPU fleet, along with process improvements that brought new capacity online earlier, contributed to Azure’s fourth-quarter performance. Hood said the additional Azure capacity delivered during the quarter was quickly monetised.

AI raises infrastructure demands

Microsoft’s Fairwater AI data centre design uses a network built to connect hundreds of thousands of Nvidia GB200 and GB300 GPUs across its Azure AI infrastructure.

Microsoft said Fairwater can operate at about 140 kilowatts per rack and 1.36 megawatts per row. The facility uses a closed-loop liquid cooling system that continuously reuses coolant after its initial fill.

Fairwater’s backend uses a two-tier Ethernet network capable of 800Gbps GPU-to-GPU connectivity. Microsoft has also built a dedicated AI wide-area network to connect AI data centres across different locations.

Microsoft is also deploying its own AI silicon alongside accelerators supplied by companies including Nvidia and AMD. Its Maia 200 inference system uses a two-tier Ethernet architecture designed to scale clusters to as many as 6,144 accelerators and incorporates Microsoft’s second-generation closed-loop liquid cooling hardware.

Based on Bloomberg’s reported figures, moving from 12GW to 38GW would add about 26GW to Microsoft’s current data centre footprint. Microsoft is already developing a 2GW data centre campus in Pecos, Texas.

Microsoft said in June that the Pecos development would add approximately 2GW to its global data centre capacity, describing it as one of the largest single capacity additions in its history. The multibillion-dollar campus is expected to be developed over five to seven years.

The planned Pecos capacity is equivalent to less than one-tenth of the roughly 26GW of additional capacity implied by Bloomberg’s reported 2032 target. Data centre developments vary in size and design, so the comparison does not translate directly into a specific number of additional campuses.

Power and spending scale up

Microsoft said in February that it had contracted 40GW of new renewable energy capacity across 26 countries since 2020 through more than 400 agreements with utilities and developers.

Of that contracted renewable capacity, 19GW was operational as of February, with the remaining projects scheduled to come online over the following five years. Microsoft also said it had reached its target of matching its annual global electricity consumption with renewable energy in 2025.

The reported 38GW data centre figure and Microsoft’s 40GW renewable energy portfolio are not directly comparable. The former refers to reported data centre power capacity, while the latter refers to the rated generating capacity of renewable energy projects contracted across multiple grids and countries.

The Pecos development will also include dedicated power infrastructure. Microsoft said the 2GW campus will initially use a co-located natural gas power facility operating behind the meter, supplying electricity directly to the site rather than drawing that power from the public grid.

Microsoft expects the power facility and data centre eventually to connect to the wider regional grid. The campus will also use closed-loop cooling, which requires an initial water fill but is designed to avoid additional water consumption during normal cooling operations.

The International Energy Agency estimates that data centres consumed about 415 terawatt-hours of electricity globally in 2024 and projects consumption to reach around 945TWh by 2030 under its base case.

The IEA expects electricity use from accelerated servers, primarily associated with AI, to grow by around 30% annually through 2030 and account for almost half of the net increase in global data centre electricity consumption. Conventional server electricity use is projected to grow at about 9% annually.

The IEA said data centres and the energy infrastructure supporting them also operate on different development timelines. A data centre can become operational in around two to three years, while new power generation and grid infrastructure generally require longer planning and construction periods.

Microsoft also has a long-term power purchase agreement with Constellation Energy supporting the restart of the 835MW Crane Clean Energy Center in Pennsylvania. The nuclear facility was previously known as Three Mile Island Unit 1.

Infrastructure spending remains a large part of Microsoft’s investment programme. Capital expenditure reached $41 billion in its fiscal fourth quarter.

About two-thirds of that spending went to shorter-lived assets, primarily CPUs and GPUs. Microsoft also recorded $5.6 billion in finance leases during the quarter, primarily for large data centre sites.

Microsoft expects capital expenditure of about $175 billion for calendar 2026 after an accounting change that will move more future data centre leases from finance leases to operating leases. The company said the change affects the accounting treatment of those leases rather than its underlying calendar-year investment plans.
